definition: Feudalism means a medieval system in which land was held from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word feudalism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know feudalism should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The seminar's first slide reduced feudalism to one line: land flows down, loyalty and service flow up.
A hierarchy is the milder arrangement — ranks above and below, as any office has; feudalism binds far tighter, bundling land, loyalty, and livelihood into one inherited package.
Serfdom is harsher than feudalism as a whole: the serf at the system's floor could not lawfully leave the land, while a knight within feudalism held real rights beside his duties.

Vassalage is the bond of service itself — one man kneeling to one lord, owing loyalty in exchange for land or protection. Feudalism is the whole system built from thousands of such bonds, stacked rank on rank from crown to plowman, with land tenure and inherited duty bundled in.

Manorialism is the economic half — the manor, its fields, and the peasants who work them for their lord. Feudalism covers far more: the entire chain of loyalty and landholding running from the crown down through every rank, of which each manor is only one small link.

Feudalism means a medieval system in which land was held from a lord in exchange for service and loyalty.

Feudalism in the shogun's Japan ran on the same engine as Europe's: a daimyo held his province from the shogun, samurai held stipends from the daimyo, and every rank owed the one above it soldiers in war and rice in peace.
Feudalism names a whole system, not a single custom — land tenure, sworn loyalty, and inherited duty bundled together.
Used of a modern office ('pure feudalism in accounting'), it is a jab: favors flowing up, patronage trickling down, and no way out by merit.
Feudalism names the specific medieval bundle — land from a lord, service and loyalty back, generation after generation.
Historians use it precisely; modern speakers borrow it as a jab at any workplace run on favors and fealty.
Both uses work, but know which one you are making.

This, he said, was feudalism — not a single king's whim but a whole society arranged as one long chain of land given down and duty owed up.

'Then he loses the land,' Mr.
